doc.title: Mike Longo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2019

title: Dizzy thought rhythm and thought piano
summary: Dizzy put notes to rhythms, thought like a pianist, and shared Stravinsky's idea that music is waiting to be uncovered.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: I’m glad you brought that up. I’ve seen — it’s pretty common nowadays in jazz ed and the magazines, they’ll take someone’s solo and someone will transcribe it, and then they’ll analyze it, much as I recall analyzing Bach back in music school. And they’ll say something like, “Notice how Dizzy hit the sharp 4 here” and they seem to be saying he did it on purpose.
No. What Dizzy used to say is he thinks rhythm and puts notes to the rhythms.

He thinks rhythm and puts notes to the rhythm. He told this lady in Florida, “Find yourself a rhythm and hang some notes on it.” So Dizzy, you know the tune “Champ”? [scats]. That’s the way he’s thinking. And he just put notes to the — now the notes, you might be looking up a scale, you might be looking up an arpeggio, you might be looking — but you’re playing the rhythms. And that’s the way Dizzy thought, and he also didn’t think trumpet, he thought piano. The first time Miles heard Dizzy and I play together he said, “It sounds like you cats got married.” Because I could see oh here he comes, let me move my fingers out of the way, because he was watching my hands on the keyboard in his head. So Dizzy didn’t think trumpet. That’s what’s fooling all the guys that try to play like Dizzy. They’re thinking trumpet. He was thinking the piano man. He knew the piano. And I remember once Miles coming over to Dizzy’s pad with one of Dizzy’s records. He said, “Right there, what is that stuff?” And Dizzy went, “See right here? I keep telling you you’ve got to learn the piano.” Which he did. And so Dizzy was a stickler about horn players. You have to be able to see music as well as play it man. And so Dizzy could play piano. I used to get pissed off — oh pardon, mad at him on the gig because he’d always be playing and like all the other guys could bring their horn into the hotel room and practice. The piano player — the only time I got to practice was before the curtain would go up. And there Dizzy’d be sitting at the piano, I said oh man. But he could sound like Monk. He played the piano like Monk. He knew the instrument man. He knew, somehow taught himself voice leading perfectly, like Bach, which goes to show you that that stuff is just natural laws man. There’s a term Stravinsky used called “ontology.” “Ontological music.” If you look up the word in the dictionary it’s a metaphysical term based on the science of existence. But in a musical sense Stravinsky is the first I heard use © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

“ontological music.” What he meant by that was the music is out there, he more or less uncovers the music rather than composes it. It’s already out there. And Dizzy used to say the same thing in his way. He would say, “Man this music is just out here waiting for someone to come get it.” And he used to tell me, he’d say “If the music tells you, you go where the music is.”
